title: YOUR BODY IS A TEMPLE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT—What Does That Have to Do With Sex?
paragraphs: YOUR BODY IS A TEMPLE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT—What Does That Have to Do With Sex?

You may have heard this verse used against tattoos, alcohol, food, or unhealthy habits. But when Paul originally wrote it, he was talking about something far more intimate—and what he said about your body, your sexuality, your shame, and the blood of Jesus changes everything.
There are some Bible verses we know so well that we can quote them without remembering why they were written.
“Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.”
You have probably heard it.
Maybe someone said it while talking about smoking.
Maybe tattoos.
Maybe overeating.
Maybe exercise.
Maybe taking care of yourself.
And certainly, the truth that our bodies belong to God has implications for how we treat them.
But open your Bible.
Read what comes immediately before 1 Corinthians 6:19–20.
Suddenly the room gets uncomfortable.
Because Paul was talking about sex.
Not abstract theology.
Not gym memberships.
Not diets.
Sex.
Sexual desire.
Sexual sin.
What happens when a person who belongs to Jesus takes the body that belongs to Christ into sexual immorality.
And perhaps that makes this passage uncomfortable for you for another reason.
Because maybe you are not reading about somebody else's past.
Maybe you are remembering yours.
A bedroom.
A hotel room.
A relationship you knew was crossing boundaries.
A screen you keep returning to when nobody is watching.
Messages you delete.
Pictures you would panic if someone discovered.
A relationship you keep calling “complicated” because calling it sin would require you to make a decision.
Maybe your story is not dramatic at all.
Maybe you simply gave somebody something you thought would make them stay.
You wanted affection.
You wanted to feel chosen.
You wanted somebody to hold you.
You wanted one night where loneliness stopped screaming.
And afterward...
they left.
Or perhaps they stayed, but something inside you changed.
Now here comes Christianity talking about sexual holiness, and immediately you expect condemnation.
You expect someone to point a finger.
You expect another sermon telling you how dirty you became.
But listen carefully.
Paul's argument is far more powerful than:
“Sex is bad.”
That is not Christianity.
The Bible does not teach that sex itself is dirty.
God created human beings male and female. Genesis presents the marital union of husband and wife as “one flesh.” Scripture can speak beautifully and positively about marital intimacy.
Sex is not Satan's invention that Christianity reluctantly tolerates.
It belongs inside God's design.
And because it is sacred, Scripture refuses to treat it as meaningless.
That is where 1 Corinthians 6 becomes breathtaking.
Paul writes:
To de sōma ou tē porneia alla tō Kyriō.
“The body is not for sexual immorality, but for the Lord.”
Notice what Paul does NOT say.
He does not merely say:
Your body is not for sexual immorality.
He says:
Your body is for the Lord.
That changes everything.
Christian sexual holiness is not ultimately about God standing over your shoulder trying to prevent you from enjoying your body.
It begins with belonging.
Your body has a purpose greater than appetite.
Your sexuality has a purpose greater than pleasure.
Your deepest identity is greater than who desires you, who rejected you, who slept with you, who touched you, what you watched, what you did, or what was done to you.
Your body is for the Lord.
Then Paul goes further.
He asks:
“Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?”
Think about those words.
If you belong to Christ, Christianity does not teach that Jesus merely saved some invisible spiritual portion of you while your physical body remains disconnected from Him.
Your body matters to Christ.
So much that Paul connects Christian hope to bodily resurrection.
God raised Jesus, Paul says, and He will also raise us by His power.
Your body therefore isn't disposable packaging around your soul.
God intends resurrection.
Then Paul discusses sexual union and reaches back to Genesis:
“The two shall become one flesh.”
This is why biblical Christianity cannot reduce sex to:
“Two consenting adults did something pleasurable, so what difference does it make?”
Consent matters enormously because coercion and abuse violate another person's dignity. But biblical sexual ethics asks another question too:
What did God create sexual union to mean?
Sex involves the body in a profoundly personal union.
Paul therefore commands something startlingly direct:
“φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.”
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not negotiate with it.
Not see how close you can stand to the edge.
Not keep the conversation because you enjoy the attention.
Not keep the app because you promise yourself you will only look.
Not maintain the secret relationship while praying for God to somehow make it holy.
Flee.
The Greek verb pheugete carries exactly that force: flee, escape, get away.
And the word translated “sexual immorality” is porneia—πορνεία—a broad New Testament term for illicit sexual activity.
Paul is not embarrassed about commanding Christians to run.
Sometimes spiritual maturity looks remarkably undramatic.
Close the browser.
Delete the conversation.
Leave the room.
End the affair.
Stop feeding the fantasy.
Tell somebody trustworthy.
Put distance between yourself and what repeatedly pulls you away from Christ.
Run.
Not because sexual temptation proves you are beyond grace.
Run because you belong to Someone.
And then comes the verse so many Christians have heard outside its context:
“ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίου πνεύματός ἐστιν”
Ē ouk oidate hoti to sōma hymōn naos tou en hymin hagiou pneumatos estin...
“Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you...?”
The word translated “temple” is ναός — naos.
Paul's language is astonishing.
He is telling believers that the Holy Spirit dwells within them.
Think about what that means.
You keep calling yourself disgusting.
God calls the redeemed body His dwelling place.
You keep defining yourself by what happened in your past.
Paul points toward Who lives within the believer now.
You keep saying:
“But you don't know what I've done.”
Maybe not.
But Jesus does.
Every hidden night.
Every compromise.
Every relapse.
Every person.
Every screen.
Every fantasy.
Every betrayal.
Every moment you promised God, “Never again,” only to find yourself crying the same prayer weeks later.
Jesus knows.
And still the Gospel says something almost impossible to believe:
There is grace for repentant sinners.
This is where sexual purity teaching can become distorted.
Some people were taught purity as though virginity itself were salvation.
As though someone who had sexual sin in their past became permanently damaged goods.
As though Jesus could forgive murderers, persecutors, thieves, liars, and rebels...
but somehow sexual sinners remained spiritually stained forever.
That is not the Gospel.
Paul had already reminded the Corinthians what some of them once were, including people whose former lives involved sexual sin.
Then comes one of the most beautiful reversals in the chapter:
“But you were washed...”
Washed.
Not tolerated.
Washed.
Not permanently labeled by the worst thing you ever did.
Washed.
Paul continues that they were sanctified and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
The church at Corinth was not a museum filled with people who had never been sexually broken.
It was a community of people Jesus was redeeming.
And maybe somebody needs that sentence desperately today.
Your sexual past does not have greater cleansing power than the blood of Jesus.
Read that again.
Your sexual past does not have greater cleansing power than the blood of Jesus.
If you have genuinely turned to Christ in repentance and faith, your identity is not “the adulterer.”
Not “the porn addict.”
Not “the promiscuous one.”
Not “the person who gave themselves away.”
Not “the person who crossed the line.”
Not “the person everybody would reject if they knew.”
And if sexual violence or abuse was committed against you, someone else's sin against your body did not make you morally guilty for what they chose to do to you.
Your identity is not what someone did to you.
Jesus Christ does not stand before broken people holding a permanent label containing their worst moment.
The Gospel announces that sinners can be forgiven, cleansed, reconciled to God, and made new through Christ.
But grace does not mean sexual sin suddenly stops mattering.
Grace is not Jesus saying:
“It doesn't matter what you do with your body.”
Grace says something infinitely greater:
“You belong to Me now.”
Paul continues:
“καὶ οὐκ ἐστὲ ἑαυτῶν”
Kai ouk este heautōn.
“You are not your own.”
That sentence collides violently with modern assumptions about freedom.
“My body, my choice.”
“My desires, my rules.”
“My bedroom, nobody else's business.”
Christianity introduces another category:
Lordship.
The Christian cannot ultimately say, “My body belongs to me.”
But neither does your body belong to the boyfriend pressuring you.
Or the girlfriend threatening to leave.
Or the husband demanding what is coercive or degrading.
Or the person manipulating your loneliness.
Or pornography.
Or your impulses.
Or your past.
Your body belongs to Christ.
And Paul tells us why:
“ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς”
Ēgorasthēte gar timēs.
“For you were bought with a price.”
There it is.
The Cross enters the bedroom.
You were bought with a price.
What price?
Not silver.
Not gold.
The New Testament's larger Gospel witness points us toward Jesus Christ giving Himself for sinners.
His body wounded.
His blood poured out.
The sinless Son of God crucified.
Buried.
Risen.
Your body matters because His body was given for your redemption.
Suddenly Christian sexual ethics is not merely a collection of prohibitions.
It becomes worship.
Paul finishes:
“δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.”
Doxasate dē ton Theon en tō sōmati hymōn.
“Therefore glorify God in your body.”
That is the destination.
Not merely:
“Stop having sinful sex.”
Glorify God in your body.
Your eyes can glorify God.
Your hands can glorify God.
Your sexuality can glorify God.
Your singleness can glorify God.
Your marriage can glorify God.
Your boundaries can glorify God.
Your repentance can glorify God.
Even your decision tonight to walk away from something nobody else knows about can become worship.
Maybe you already failed.
Then hear this carefully.
The answer is not pretending.
The answer is repentance.
And repentance is not self-hatred.
Biblical repentance is a turning.
You stop defending what God calls sin.
You stop renaming darkness so you can remain comfortable inside it.
You bring it into the light.
You confess.
You turn.
You receive mercy through Christ.
And you begin walking differently.
Perhaps tonight that means telling someone:
“We can't keep doing this.”
Perhaps it means confessing an affair.
Perhaps it means installing accountability around pornography and inviting a mature believer into the struggle instead of fighting alone.
Perhaps it means ending a secret online relationship.
Perhaps it means admitting that what you have called “love” has repeatedly required disobedience to Jesus.
Perhaps it simply means falling to your knees and finally saying:
“Jesus... I have been trying to belong to You while keeping this part of myself for me.”
And maybe there will be tears.
Let them come.
Because conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Conviction says:
Come out of hiding.
Condemnation whispers:
Stay hidden because God could never want you now.
The Gospel answers:
Jesus already knew exactly what kind of sinner He was rescuing.
You do not clean yourself enough to become worthy of the Cross.
You come to the Cross because you cannot clean yourself.
That is grace.
Not cheap grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace that forgives you and then begins changing you.
Grace that meets you in the wreckage without promising to leave you there.
Grace that teaches your desires they are no longer your master.
Grace that teaches your body:
You belong to Jesus now.
Maybe you have carried sexual shame for ten years.
Twenty years.
Forty years.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you became the respectable Christian.
You serve.
You smile.
You quote Scripture.
You worship with everyone else.
But somewhere inside you is still that frightened younger version of yourself thinking:
“If everybody knew, they wouldn't look at me the same.”
Maybe they wouldn't.
But Jesus already knows.
And He went to the Cross with His eyes open.
That is why our message will always be:
Not because scandal does not matter.
Not because sin is harmless.
But because scandal does not get the final word when Jesus Christ enters the story.
Peter's denial did not get the final word.
Paul's persecution of Christians did not get the final word.
The Corinthians' former sins did not get the final word.
And if you belong to Jesus, your worst sexual failure does not get to write the final sentence either.
Jesus does.
Maybe today is the day you stop hiding.
You do not have to publish the details of your private struggle. Wisdom still matters. But sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And if Christ has already brought you through sexual brokenness, shame, addiction, adultery, pornography, or a past you thought would destroy you, consider commenting “Christ is still healing me.”
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need to know that repentance is possible.
That restoration is possible.
That obedience is possible.
That Jesus still saves.
And please don't keep this article imprisoned on your screen.
Send it privately to the person who has been trying to come back to God.
It does not.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
It cannot.

Christians and churches differ in how they understand the application of biblical tithing under the New Covenant, and believers should give prayerfully, willingly, generously, and without manipulation.
Support Gospel Warrior because you believe Christ-centered truth should keep reaching people.
Support it as an offering of generosity if God leads you to do so.
It is mission.

If these resources help you know Christ, understand Scripture, fight sin, strengthen your family, disciple someone else, or return to God after wandering, then helping sustain and expand that work can itself be an act of Christian generosity.
And even if you cannot financially support Gospel Warrior, you can still help.
Your share costs nothing, but it may place the Gospel in front of someone we could never reach ourselves.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the Christian who has grown cold.
Invite the believer secretly fighting pornography.
Invite the person carrying sexual shame.
Invite the seeker who thinks Christianity is nothing but rules.
Invite even the unbeliever who has never understood why Christians believe the human body matters.
Because maybe they do not need another Christian shouting at them about sex.
Maybe they need to discover why Jesus thought sinners were worth dying for.
And perhaps that is what you needed too.
You thought this article was going to tell you what you were forbidden to do with your body.
Instead, Scripture brought us somewhere deeper.
Your body is not worthless.
Your body is not merely an appetite machine.
Your body is not merchandise.
Your body is not the property of whoever desires it.
Your body is not permanently defined by whoever violated it.
Your body is not disposable.
For the Christian, your body belongs to Christ.
The Holy Spirit dwells within you.
You were bought with a price.
Therefore...
glorify God in your body.
So when temptation whispers tonight,
“Nobody will know...”
remember:
This isn't ultimately about who is watching.
It is about Whose you are.
When shame whispers,
“After what you did, God could never use you...”
remember the Cross.
When your past whispers,
“This is who you will always be...”
remember the empty tomb.
And when Jesus calls you out of sexual sin, do not hear the voice of a God trying to steal your joy.
Hear the voice of the Savior who paid for you saying:
You were made for more than this. Come home.
Because perhaps the most devastating lie sexual sin ever told you was that after everything you had done, Jesus would no longer want you.
But the hands that were pierced for sinners are still reaching into places shame told you God would never enter.
